name: Athleisure

card.summary: Athletic-style clothing (leggings, joggers, hoodies, technical tees) worn as everyday dress, used to look fit, put-together and comfortable outside the gym.
card.note: Research links activewear engagement with both fitness behaviour and body-image pressure in some women.

quick.overview:
Athleisure is a clothing style built from workout apparel worn in daily life: leggings, joggers, hoodies, performance tees and athletic sneakers. Fitted stretch fabrics show off a trained physique, and the look signals an active lifestyle.

Wikipedia traces it from Champion hoodies and the spread of spandex through tracksuit street fashion to a recognised retail category in the mid-2010s. Studies of women who wear it describe feeling more confident and athletic, and also more aware of how their body matches fitness ideals.
quick.how: People wear it by pairing technical or stretch pieces with everyday items, choosing fit and colour to flatter the body, and treating the same outfit as gym-to-street clothing. Lululemon, Adidas, Nike and many mass retailers sell it.
quick.risks: There are no physical risks beyond comfort and fit. A 2026 survey study found activewear engagement correlated with idealised body aspirations, appearance comparison and self-objectification alongside fitness behaviours, and a 2020 interview study reported mixed feelings. Critics also raise environmental concerns about synthetic fabrics and chemical finishes.

lead: Athleisure is a clothing category and style in which athletic-inspired apparel is worn as everyday clothing. Its name combines 'athletic' and 'leisure' [1]. Fitted, stretchy, moisture-wicking garments such as leggings, joggers and hoodies are worn to work, travel and social settings as well as the gym [1][2].

For people working on their appearance, athleisure is a way to present a physique. A Body Image study of 20 women described it as clothing that accentuates the wearer's physique and communicates adherence to a fit lifestyle, with participants saying it made them feel more confident and athletic [3]. Technical fabrics also offer comfort and durability, which is why people choose it for all-day wear [1].
Research is mainly qualitative and survey-based, focused on women. It reports positive links with fitness behaviour and confidence and also links with body-image pressure [3][4].

angle.text: The garments themselves change how a body is displayed and how the wearer is read by others: fitted athletic cuts emphasise shape, and the outfit signals an active lifestyle. People use it as a comfortable everyday style that carries a gym-fit image.

paras: Athleisure refers to hybrid clothing that is athletic in cut and fabric but designed for everyday wear. Grokipedia describes the hallmarks as elastic waistbands, seamless construction and stretch fabrics that hold up under varied activity [1]. A 2020 Body Image paper defines it as athletic-inspired workout apparel that explicitly accentuates the wearer's physique [3].

Wikipedia traces the lineage to Champion hoodies for laborers in the 1930s, DuPont's invention of spandex in 1958, Adidas tracksuits in 1963, athletic street fashion in the 1970s and 1980s spread by hip-hop videos, and yoga pants in the mid-to-late 2000s. By the mid-2010s athleisure was a recognised retail category, with demand boosted again by the COVID-19 pandemic [2]. Grokipedia adds earlier sportswear history, including Jean Patou's 1921 tennis dress for Suzanne Lenglen and the 1980s aerobics boom [1].
Wikipedia cites market estimates of about $35 billion in US sales in 2014 and about $155 billion worldwide in 2018, and describes celebrities such as Beyoncé and Rihanna as promoting the style [2].

In style-focused discussions the appeal is looking athletic and fitted without effort, and gym-wear brands are often chosen for how they display muscle and shape. Research on the style itself has concentrated on women: wearing athleisure was linked to feeling confident, to being motivated toward fitspiration-style activities, and to awareness of whether one's body matches the thin-fit ideal [3].

A 2026 survey study of 455 students and 374 community members found that 40 to 87 per cent of women engaged with activewear in some form, that 30 per cent felt self-conscious at least half the time they wore it, and that it was worn for exercise less than half the time; engagement correlated with fitness behaviours and also with idealised appearance aspirations and self-objectification [4]. Wikipedia reports critics who say the style emphasises the female form and raise environmental concerns about dyes, solvents and petroleum-based materials [2]. A 2021 paper analysed everyday activewear practices through a new-materialist lens, including laundering and environmental impact [5].
No studies found. Related research on the clothing trend consists of qualitative interviews and surveys on body image [3][4].

timeline.event: Jean Patou designs a pleated tennis outfit for Suzanne Lenglen [1].
Jane Fonda's workout video helps popularise leggings and leotards [1].
Athleisure becomes a recognised retail category [2].
